The **96th Academy Awards** ceremony, presented by the [Academy of Motion
Picture Arts and Sciences](/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences
"Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences") (AMPAS), took place on March
10, 2024, at the [Dolby Theatre](/wiki/Dolby_Theatre "Dolby Theatre") in
[Hollywood, Los Angeles](/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los
Angeles"). During the gala, the AMPAS presented Academy Awards (commonly
referred to as Oscars) in 23 categories honoring [films released in
2023](/wiki/2023_in_film "2023 in film"). The ceremony, televised in the
United States by [ABC](/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American
Broadcasting Company"), was produced by Raj Kapoor and Katy Mullan, and was
directed by [Hamish Hamilton](/wiki/Hamish_Hamilton_\(director\) "Hamish
Hamilton \(director\)").[2][5] Comedian [Jimmy Kimmel](/wiki/Jimmy_Kimmel
"Jimmy Kimmel") hosted the show for the fourth time. He first presided over
the [89th ceremony](/wiki/89th_Academy_Awards "89th Academy Awards") held in
2017, and had most recently hosted the [previous year's
ceremony](/wiki/95th_Academy_Awards "95th Academy Awards").[6]

In related events, the Academy held its 14th [Governors
Awards](/wiki/Governors_Awards "Governors Awards") ceremony at the Ray Dolby
Ballroom of the [Ovation Hollywood](/wiki/Ovation_Hollywood "Ovation
Hollywood") complex in Hollywood, on January 9, 2024.[7] The [Academy
Scientific and Technical Awards](/wiki/Academy_Scientific_and_Technical_Award
"Academy Scientific and Technical Award") were presented by host [Natasha
Lyonne](/wiki/Natasha_Lyonne "Natasha Lyonne") on February 23, 2024, in a
ceremony at the [Academy Museum of Motion
Pictures](/wiki/Academy_Museum_of_Motion_Pictures "Academy Museum of Motion
Pictures") in Los Angeles.[8]

_[Oppenheimer](/wiki/Oppenheimer_\(film\) "Oppenheimer \(film\)")_ won seven
awards, including [Best Picture](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy
Award for Best Picture").[9] Other winners included _[Poor
Things](/wiki/Poor_Things_\(film\) "Poor Things \(film\)")_ with four awards,
_[The Zone of Interest](/wiki/The_Zone_of_Interest_\(film\) "The Zone of
Interest \(film\)")_ with two, and _[American
Fiction](/wiki/American_Fiction_\(film\) "American Fiction \(film\)")_ ,
_[Anatomy of a Fall](/wiki/Anatomy_of_a_Fall "Anatomy of a Fall")_ ,
_[Barbie](/wiki/Barbie_\(film\) "Barbie \(film\)")_ , _[The Boy and the
Heron](/wiki/The_Boy_and_the_Heron "The Boy and the Heron")_ , _[Godzilla
Minus One](/wiki/Godzilla_Minus_One "Godzilla Minus One")_ , _[The
Holdovers](/wiki/The_Holdovers "The Holdovers")_ , _[The Last Repair
Shop](/wiki/The_Last_Repair_Shop "The Last Repair Shop")_ , _[20 Days in
Mariupol](/wiki/20_Days_in_Mariupol "20 Days in Mariupol")_ , _[War Is
Over!](/wiki/War_Is_Over! "War Is Over!")_ , and _[The Wonderful Story of
Henry Sugar](/wiki/The_Wonderful_Story_of_Henry_Sugar_\(film\) "The Wonderful
Story of Henry Sugar \(film\)")_ with one.[10] The telecast drew 19.49 million
viewers in the United States.[4]

The nominees for the 96th Academy Awards were announced on January 23, 2024,
at the [Samuel Goldwyn Theater](/wiki/Samuel_Goldwyn_Theater "Samuel Goldwyn
Theater") in Beverly Hills, by actress [Zazie Beetz](/wiki/Zazie_Beetz "Zazie
Beetz") and actor [Jack Quaid](/wiki/Jack_Quaid "Jack Quaid").[11]
_[Oppenheimer](/wiki/Oppenheimer_\(film\) "Oppenheimer \(film\)")_ led all
nominees with thirteen nominations; _[Poor Things](/wiki/Poor_Things_\(film\)
"Poor Things \(film\)")_ came in second with eleven.[12] The winners were
announced during the awards ceremony on March 10.[13]

_Oppenheimer_ was the first Best Picture winner to also win both male acting
awards since 1959's _[Ben-Hur](/wiki/Ben-Hur_\(1959_film\) "Ben-Hur \(1959
film\)")_.[14] For the first time in Oscar history, three Best Picture
nominees were directed by women.[15] At age 81, [Martin
Scorsese](/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese") became the oldest Best
Director nominee in Oscar history.[16] Best Actress nominee [Lily
Gladstone](/wiki/Lily_Gladstone "Lily Gladstone") was the first US-born Native
American person nominated in that category.[17] The 49-year gap between
[Robert De Niro](/wiki/Robert_De_Niro "Robert De Niro")'s first nomination for
_[The Godfather Part II](/wiki/The_Godfather_Part_II "The Godfather Part II")_
and his latest for _[Killers of the Flower
Moon](/wiki/Killers_of_the_Flower_Moon_\(film\) "Killers of the Flower Moon
\(film\)")_ set the record for longest gap between first and most recent
career Oscar nominations.[18] Having previously won for composing the [titular
song](/wiki/No_Time_to_Die_\(song\) "No Time to Die \(song\)") for 2021's _[No
Time to Die](/wiki/No_Time_to_Die "No Time to Die")_ , Best Original Song co-
winner [Billie Eilish](/wiki/Billie_Eilish "Billie Eilish") became the
youngest person to win two Oscars.[19] Best Sound winner _[The Zone of
Interest](/wiki/The_Zone_of_Interest_\(film\) "The Zone of Interest
\(film\)")_ and Best Visual Effects winner _[Godzilla Minus
One](/wiki/Godzilla_Minus_One "Godzilla Minus One")_ were the first non-
English language films to win their respective categories.[20]

### Governors Awards

The Academy held its 14th annual [Governors Awards](/wiki/Governors_Awards
"Governors Awards") ceremony on January 9, 2024, during which the following
awards were presented:[23]

#### Honorary Awards

  * To [Angela Bassett](/wiki/Angela_Bassett "Angela Bassett"), who has inspired audiences around the world with her powerful and fearless performances.[24]
  * To [Mel Brooks](/wiki/Mel_Brooks "Mel Brooks"), for his comedic brilliance, producing acumen and expansive body of work. [24]
  * To [Carol Littleton](/wiki/Carol_Littleton "Carol Littleton"), whose commitment to her craft has significantly elevated the art of film editing.[24]

#### Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award

  * [Michelle Satter](/wiki/Michelle_Satter "Michelle Satter") - "For her unwavering support of filmmakers and commitment to the independent filmmaking community."[25]

## Ceremony information

[![Photo of Jimmy Kimmel in June
2022](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Jimmy_Kimmel_June_2022.jpg/250px-
Jimmy_Kimmel_June_2022.jpg)](/wiki/File:Jimmy_Kimmel_June_2022.jpg)[Jimmy
Kimmel](/wiki/Jimmy_Kimmel "Jimmy Kimmel") hosted the 96th Academy Awards.

In October 2023, the Academy hired [television
producers](/wiki/Television_producer "Television producer") Raj Kapoor and
Katy Mullan to oversee production of the 2024 ceremony with veteran television
director [Hamish Hamilton](/wiki/Hamish_Hamilton_\(director\) "Hamish Hamilton
\(director\)") selected to direct the telecast.[27] "Raj and Hamish have been
incredible Oscars collaborators, and we are delighted to welcome them and Katy
to lead the 96th Oscars," said AMPAS CEO [Bill
Kramer](/wiki/Bill_Kramer_\(executive\) "Bill Kramer \(executive\)") and AMPAS
President [Janet Yang](/wiki/Janet_Yang "Janet Yang") in a press release
justifying their selection of the producers. "Their deep love of cinema, fresh
vision, and tremendous live television expertise is perfect for our
reinvigorated show."[28] In response, Kapoor and Mullan released a statement
saying, "As a Canadian boy of South Asian descent and a girl from London who
grew up watching the Oscars, dreaming of being part of it, this is a 'pinch
me' moment! This has been an exceptional year for the movies, and it's an
absolute privilege to be leading the team celebrating the global film industry
and the astounding talents that bring these cinematic stories to life. We're
dedicated to making it a remarkable celebration for all."[29]

The following month, comedian and talk show host [Jimmy
Kimmel](/wiki/Jimmy_Kimmel "Jimmy Kimmel") was announced as host of the gala,
and his wife Molly McNearney was hired to join Kapoor and Mullan as a co-
producer.[30] Kapoor and Mullan explained their reason to bring back the
veteran comedian and talk show host saying, "Jimmy has cemented himself as one
of the all-time great Oscars hosts with his perfect blend of humanity and
humor, and Molly is one of the best live TV producers around. We are delighted
to be working with them and their teams on the show."[31] Kimmel responded to
his selection as host in a press release retorting, "I always dreamed of
hosting the Oscars exactly four times."[32]

In an effort to increase ratings and viewership, the Academy and ABC announced
that the ceremony's start time would be moved ahead by an hour to 4:00 p.m.
[PT](/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") (7:00 p.m.
[ET](/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone")).[33] Producers hoped that
the earlier start time would result in winners in major categories being
announced earlier in the evening and would therefore mitigate declining
viewership on the East Coast.[2] As a result of the changes, the red carpet
pre-show that precedes the main telecast was shortened to 30 minutes from its
usual 90 minute runtime. ABC would also have the ability to air a primetime
program as a lead-out for the ceremony at 7:30 p.m. PT (10:30 p.m. ET), with
the network scheduling a new episode of its sitcom _[Abbott
Elementary](/wiki/Abbott_Elementary "Abbott Elementary")_.[34]

Several others participated in the production of the ceremony and related
events. Production designers Misty Buckley and Alana Billingsley designed a
new stage for the show. According to Buckley and Billingsley, the stage was
designed to "create a modern plaza that invites people in."[35] Furthermore,
the set utilized several columns that subtly changed images during several
awards presentations such as typewriters for screenwriters for the screenplay
categories and sketches of the Best Costume Design nominees for the
aforementioned category.[36] Musician [Rickey Minor](/wiki/Rickey_Minor
"Rickey Minor") was the musical director for the ceremony.[37] Comedian and
journalist [Amelia Dimoldenberg](/wiki/Amelia_Dimoldenberg "Amelia
Dimoldenberg") served as a social media and red carpet correspondent,
interviewing nominees at events including the Oscars nominees lunch and
hosting videos showcasing behind the scenes preparations leading up the
ceremony.[38] In addition, Dimoldenberg and internet personality Reece Feldman
interviewed nominees and guests of the ceremony on platforms such as
[Facebook](/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") and [TikTok](/wiki/TikTok "TikTok").[39]
Choreographer [Mandy Moore](/wiki/Mandy_Moore_\(choreographer\) "Mandy Moore
\(choreographer\)") oversaw production of [Ryan Gosling](/wiki/Ryan_Gosling
"Ryan Gosling") and [Mark Ronson](/wiki/Mark_Ronson "Mark Ronson")'s
performance of "[I'm Just Ken](/wiki/I%27m_Just_Ken "I'm Just Ken")" which
paid homage to the song "[Diamonds Are a Girl's Best
Friend](/wiki/Diamonds_Are_a_Girl%27s_Best_Friend "Diamonds Are a Girl's Best
Friend")" from the film _[Gentlemen Prefer
Blondes](/wiki/Gentlemen_Prefer_Blondes_\(1953_film\) "Gentlemen Prefer
Blondes \(1953 film\)")_.[40] The performance utilized 62 different actors
portraying [Ken](/wiki/Ken_\(doll\) "Ken \(doll\)"), and featured cameos from
Gosling's _Barbie_ co-stars [Kingsley Ben-Adir](/wiki/Kingsley_Ben-Adir
"Kingsley Ben-Adir"), [Scott Evans](/wiki/Scott_Evans_\(actor\) "Scott Evans
\(actor\)"), [Ncuti Gatwa](/wiki/Ncuti_Gatwa "Ncuti Gatwa"), and [Simu
Liu](/wiki/Simu_Liu "Simu Liu"), and musicians [Wolfgang Van
Halen](/wiki/Wolfgang_Van_Halen "Wolfgang Van Halen") and
[Slash](/wiki/Slash_\(musician\) "Slash \(musician\)").[41]

Initially, the Governors Awards were scheduled to be held on November 18,
2023, but they were postponed by two months to January 9, 2024, due to the
[2023 Hollywood labor disputes](/wiki/2023_Hollywood_labor_disputes "2023
Hollywood labor disputes").[42] Meanwhile, actress [Michelle
Pfeiffer](/wiki/Michelle_Pfeiffer "Michelle Pfeiffer") was planned to co-
present Best Picture with her _[Scarface](/wiki/Scarface_\(1983_film\)
"Scarface \(1983 film\)")_ co-star [Al Pacino](/wiki/Al_Pacino "Al Pacino").
However, prior commitments on the [East
Coast](/wiki/East_Coast_of_the_United_States "East Coast of the United
States") prevented her from traveling in time for the ceremony, and Pacino
presented the award solo.[43]

### Best Picture nominee diversity rules

In September 2020, the Academy announced that, starting with the 96th awards,
all films submitted for Best Picture consideration must satisfy an established
set of "representation and inclusion standards".[44] In a press release, then-
AMPAS president [David Rubin](/wiki/David_Rubin_\(casting_director\) "David
Rubin \(casting director\)") and then-Academy CEO [Dawn
Hudson](/wiki/Dawn_Hudson "Dawn Hudson") said of the new standards, "The
aperture must widen to reflect our diverse global population in both the
creation of motion pictures and in the audiences who connect with them. The
Academy is committed to playing a vital role in helping make this a reality.
We believe these inclusion standards will be a catalyst for long-lasting,
essential change in our industry."[45]

According to the rules, each film would be required to satisfy at least two of
the four standards by hiring people from an "underrepresented" group namely
individuals from a racial/ethnic minority, LGBTQ+ people, or persons with a
cognitive or physical disability in order to compete in the category. Standard
A involves "On-screen representation, themes, and narratives" which deals with
a film's lead performers, cast, or subject matter. Standard B entails
"Creative leadership and department heads" which involves creative heads in a
film's production or the film's crew as a whole. Standard C encompasses
"Industry access and opportunities" which refers to both paid internships and
training opportunities. Standard D involves "Audience development" which
refers to representation in marketing, publicity, and distribution.[46]
Filmmakers would have to submit a confidential Representation and Inclusion
Standards Entry form (RAISE) indicating how their films would comply with the
standards outlined by the Academy.[47]

Three years after the new rules were announced, AMPAS released a statement
affirming that films not submitted for Best Picture consideration could bypass
submitting the RAISE forms reporting a film's gender, race, and disability
data. In addition, Academy FAQs stated that British films that have complied
with the [British Film Institute](/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British Film
Institute")'s inclusion and diversity standards would also be deemed as
satisfying the Academy's diversity requirements.[48]

### Box office performance of Best Picture nominees

When the nominations were announced, nine of the ten films nominated for Best
Picture had earned a combined gross of $1.09 billion at the American and
Canadian box offices at the time.[49] _Barbie_ was the highest-grossing film
among the Best Picture nominees with $636 million in domestic box office
receipts.[50] _Oppenheimer_ came in second with $326 million; this was
followed by _Killers of the Flower Moon_ ($67 million), _Poor Things_ ($20.4
million), _The Holdovers_ ($18.7 million), _Past Lives_ ($10.9 million),
_American Fiction_ ($7.9 million), _Anatomy of a Fall_ ($3.9 million), and
_The Zone of Interest_ ($1.6 million).[51] The official domestic box office
figures for _Maestro_ were unavailable due to their distributor
[Netflix](/wiki/Netflix "Netflix")'s policy of refusing to release such
figures.[52][53] Furthermore, with its win for Best Picture, _Oppenheimer_
became the highest-grossing winner in that category since 2003's _[The Lord of
the Rings: The Return of the
King](/wiki/The_Lord_of_the_Rings:_The_Return_of_the_King "The Lord of the
Rings: The Return of the King")_.[54]

### Critical reviews and reactions

Television critic Robert Lloyd of the _[Los Angeles
Times](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ wrote, "It was a long
night, as it always is, but not the slog it often is. The scripted banter was
better than usual, and when it failed, personality took up the slack."
Regarding Kimmel's performance as host, he commented that he was "a reliable,
relatable presence liable to stir no controversy in a venue that has a low
tolerance for controversy. At the same time he's sharp enough not to be
boring."[55] Alison Herman of _[Variety](/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety
\(magazine\)")_ remarked that despite the lack of surprises amongst the
winners, "The show delivered entertainment and emotion in spades, if not
surprise." She also commended Gosling's performance of "I'm Just Ken" as "a
maximalist, infectiously goofy singalong was the ideal way to channel the
feel-good energy of an Oscars where none of the bonhomie felt forced, as it
often can."[56] _[The Hollywood Reporter](/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The
Hollywood Reporter")_ columnist Daniel Fienberg lauded Kimmel as "A guy you
can trust to do a monologue and then he'll hold together the disparate
components and fill dead air and generally keep the mood light." He also
singled out the decision to have five previous winners presenting the nominees
in each acting category as a highlight of the festivities and acclaimed the
witty banter between co-presenters.[57]

Furthermore, _The Zone of Interest_ director, [Jonathan
Glazer](/wiki/Jonathan_Glazer "Jonathan Glazer"), received both praise and
criticism for his acceptance speech calling for an end to [Israel's
bombardment of Gaza](/wiki/Israeli_invasion_of_the_Gaza_Strip "Israeli
invasion of the Gaza Strip"). One sentence from Glazer's speech, in which he
said that he and fellow producer [James
Wilson](/wiki/James_Wilson_\(producer\) "James Wilson \(producer\)") "stand
here as men who refute their Jewishness and the [Holocaust](/wiki/Holocaust
"Holocaust") being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so
many innocent people", was widely misquoted. Some sources truncated his
remarks after the words "refute their Jewishness", suggesting that Glazer was
disavowing his [Jewish identity](/wiki/Jewish_identity "Jewish
identity").[58][59] Many pro-[Israel](/wiki/Israel "Israel") figures
disapproved of the statement, and over 1,000 Jewish members of the film
industry signed an [open letter](/wiki/Open_letter "Open letter") denouncing
Glazer's speech and defending the actions of the Israeli government.[60]
Others, including playwright [Tony Kushner](/wiki/Tony_Kushner "Tony Kushner")
and director of the [Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum](/wiki/Auschwitz-
Birkenau_State_Museum "Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum"), [Piotr
Cywiński](/wiki/Piotr_Cywi%C5%84ski "Piotr Cywiński"), defended Glazer's
comments.[61][62] One month after the ceremony took place, over 450 Jewish
members of the international film community, including [Joel
Coen](/wiki/Coen_brothers "Coen brothers"), [Elliott
Gould](/wiki/Elliott_Gould "Elliott Gould"), [Todd Haynes](/wiki/Todd_Haynes
"Todd Haynes"), [Joaquin Phoenix](/wiki/Joaquin_Phoenix "Joaquin Phoenix"),
and [Wallace Shawn](/wiki/Wallace_Shawn "Wallace Shawn"), signed an open
letter in support of Glazer's speech.[63]

### Ratings and reception

The American telecast on ABC drew in an average of 19.49 million people over
its length, which was a 4% increase from the previous year's ceremony.[64][4]
The show also held steady in [Nielsen
ratings](/wiki/Nielsen_Media_Research#Nielsen_TV_ratings "Nielsen Media
Research") compared to the previous ceremony with 9.9% of households watching
the ceremony.[65] However, it garnered a lower 18–49 demo rating with a 3.8
rating among viewers in that demographic.[66]

In July 2024, the broadcast was nominated for seven awards at the [76th
Primetime Emmys](/wiki/76th_Primetime_Emmy_Awards "76th Primetime Emmy
Awards") and its corresponding [Creative Arts Emmy
Awards](/wiki/76th_Primetime_Creative_Arts_Emmy_Awards "76th Primetime
Creative Arts Emmy Awards").[67] Two months later, the broadcast won four of
those nominations for [Outstanding Variety Special
(Live)](/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Variety_Special_\(Live\)
"Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Variety Special \(Live\)") (Executive
Producers: Raj Kapoor, Katy Mullan, and Molly McNearney; Co-Executive
Producer: Rob Paine; Producers: Taryn Hurd and Sarah Levine Hall; Host: Jimmy
Kimmel), [Outstanding Directing for a Variety
Special](/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Directing_for_a_Variety_Special
"Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Directing for a Variety Special")
(Hamish Hamilton), [Outstanding Music
Direction](/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Music_Direction
"Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Music Direction") (Rickey Minor), and
[Outstanding Production Design for a Variety
Special](/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Production_Design_for_a_Variety_Special
"Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Production Design for a Variety
Special") (Production Designers: Alana Billinglsey and Misty Buckley; Art
Directors: John Zuiker and Margaux LaPresle).[68] It marked the first time
since the [63rd ceremony](/wiki/63rd_Academy_Awards "63rd Academy Awards") in
1991, that an Academy Awards ceremony was awarded a top [Primetime Emmy
Award](/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Awards "Primetime Emmy Awards") for variety
programming.[69][70]

**Sir Christopher Edward Nolan** (born 30 July 1970) is a British and American
filmmaker. Known for his Hollywood
[blockbusters](/wiki/Blockbuster_\(entertainment\) "Blockbuster
\(entertainment\)") with structurally complex storytelling, he is considered a
leading filmmaker of the 21st century. [Nolan's
films](/wiki/Christopher_Nolan_filmography "Christopher Nolan filmography")
have earned over $6.6 billion worldwide, making him the [seventh-highest-
grossing film director](/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_film_directors "List of
highest-grossing film directors"). [His
accolades](/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Christopher_Nolan
"List of awards and nominations received by Christopher Nolan") include two
[Academy Awards](/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards"), a [Golden Globe
Award](/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award") and two [British Academy
Film Awards](/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Awards "British Academy Film Awards").
Nolan was appointed a [Commander of the Order of the British
Empire](/wiki/Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Commander of the
Order of the British Empire") in 2019 and received a
[knighthood](/wiki/Knight_Bachelor "Knight Bachelor") in 2024 for his
contributions to film.

Nolan developed an interest in filmmaking from a young age. After studying
[English literature](/wiki/English_literature "English literature") at
[University College London](/wiki/University_College_London "University
College London"), he made several short films before his feature film debut
with _[Following](/wiki/Following "Following")_ (1998). Nolan gained
international recognition with his second film,
_[Memento](/wiki/Memento_\(film\) "Memento \(film\)")_ (2000), and
transitioned into studio filmmaking with
_[Insomnia](/wiki/Insomnia_\(2002_film\) "Insomnia \(2002 film\)")_ (2002). He
became a high-profile director with [_The Dark Knight_
trilogy](/wiki/Batman_in_film#The_Dark_Knight_trilogy "Batman in film")
(2005–2012) and found further success with _[The
Prestige](/wiki/The_Prestige_\(film\) "The Prestige \(film\)")_ (2006),
_[Inception](/wiki/Inception "Inception")_ (2010),
_[Interstellar](/wiki/Interstellar_\(film\) "Interstellar \(film\)")_ (2014)
and _[Dunkirk](/wiki/Dunkirk_\(2017_film\) "Dunkirk \(2017 film\)")_ (2017).
After the release of _[Tenet](/wiki/Tenet_\(film\) "Tenet \(film\)")_ (2020),
Nolan parted ways with longtime distributor [Warner Bros.
Pictures](/wiki/Warner_Bros._Pictures "Warner Bros. Pictures") and signed with
[Universal Pictures](/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures") for the
biographical thriller _[Oppenheimer](/wiki/Oppenheimer_\(film\) "Oppenheimer
\(film\)")_ (2023), which won him Academy Awards for [Best
Director](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best
Director") and [Best Picture](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy
Award for Best Picture").

[Nolan's work](/wiki/Cinematic_style_of_Christopher_Nolan "Cinematic style of
Christopher Nolan") regularly features in the listings of best films of their
respective decades. Infused with a [metaphysical](/wiki/Metaphysical
"Metaphysical") outlook, his films thematise [epistemology](/wiki/Epistemology
"Epistemology"), [existentialism](/wiki/Existentialism "Existentialism"),
ethics, the construction of time and the malleable nature of memory and
personal identity. They feature [mathematically
inspired](/wiki/Mathematics_and_art "Mathematics and art") images and
concepts, unconventional [narrative structures](/wiki/Nonlinear_narrative
"Nonlinear narrative"), [practical special
effects](/wiki/Practical_special_effects "Practical special effects"),
experimental soundscapes, [large-format](/wiki/70_mm_film "70 mm film") film
photography and [materialistic](/wiki/Materialism "Materialism") perspectives.
His enthusiasm for the use and preservation of traditional film stock in
cinema production as opposed to digital cameras has also garnered significant
attention. He has co-written several of his films with his brother,
[Jonathan](/wiki/Jonathan_Nolan "Jonathan Nolan"), and runs the production
company [Syncopy Inc.](/wiki/Syncopy_Inc. "Syncopy Inc.") with his wife, [Emma
Thomas](/wiki/Emma_Thomas "Emma Thomas").

## Early life and education

Christopher Edward Nolan was born on 30 July 1970 in
[Westminster](/wiki/Westminster "Westminster"), London.[1][2] His father,
Brendan James Nolan, is a retired British advertising executive of Irish
descent[3] who worked as a [creative director](/wiki/Creative_director
"Creative director"). His mother, Christina Jensen, was an American flight
attendant from [Evanston, Illinois](/wiki/Evanston,_Illinois "Evanston,
Illinois"); she would later work as a teacher of English. He has an elder
brother, Matthew, and a younger brother, [Jonathan](/wiki/Jonathan_Nolan
"Jonathan Nolan"), also a filmmaker. The three brothers were raised
[Catholic](/wiki/Catholic "Catholic") in [Highgate](/wiki/Highgate "Highgate")
and spent their summers in Evanston.[4][5] Nolan also spent time living in
Chicago during his youth, and he holds both UK and US citizenship.[6][7]

[![An image showing the top of the oculus in the Flaxman Gallery, University
College
London](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Flaxman_Gallery%2C_UCL.JPG/250px-
Flaxman_Gallery%2C_UCL.JPG)](/wiki/File:Flaxman_Gallery,_UCL.JPG)Nolan
attended [University College London](/wiki/University_College_London
"University College London") and used its Flaxman Gallery for a scene in
_[Inception](/wiki/Inception "Inception")_ (2010).[8]

Growing up, Nolan was particularly influenced by the work of Sir [Ridley
Scott](/wiki/Ridley_Scott "Ridley Scott") and the science fiction films
_[2001: A Space Odyssey](/wiki/2001:_A_Space_Odyssey "2001: A Space Odyssey")_
(1968) and _[Star Wars](/wiki/Star_Wars_\(film\) "Star Wars \(film\)")_
(1977).[9][10] He would repeatedly watch the latter film and extensively
research its making.[11] Nolan began making films at the age of seven,
borrowing his father's [Super 8 camera](/wiki/Super_8_film "Super 8 film") and
shooting short films with his action figures.[12] These films included a [stop
motion animation](/wiki/Stop_motion_animation "Stop motion animation") homage
to _Star Wars_ called _Space Wars_. He cast his brother Jonathan and built
sets from "clay, flour, egg boxes and toilet rolls".[9] His uncle, who had
worked at [NASA](/wiki/NASA "NASA") building guidance systems for the
[Apollo](/wiki/Apollo_program "Apollo program") rockets, sent him some launch
footage: "I re-filmed them off the screen and cut them in, thinking no-one
would notice", Nolan later remarked.[13] From the age of 11, he aspired to be
a professional filmmaker.[14] Between 1981 and 1983, Nolan enrolled at Barrow
Hills, a Catholic prep school in [Witley](/wiki/Witley "Witley"), Surrey.[15]
In his teenage years, Nolan started making films with Adrien and [Roko
Belic](/wiki/Roko_Belic "Roko Belic"). Nolan and Roko co-directed the
[surreal](/wiki/Surrealism "Surrealism") 8 mm _Tarantella_ (1989), which was
shown on _Image Union_ , an independent film and video showcase on the [Public
Broadcasting Service](/wiki/Public_Broadcasting_Service "Public Broadcasting
Service").[a][17][18] In 2021, after a fan posted a copy of _Tarantella_
online, Nolan's production company filed a copyright infringement claim to
have the film removed.[19]

Nolan was educated at [Haileybury and Imperial Service
College](/wiki/Haileybury_and_Imperial_Service_College "Haileybury and
Imperial Service College"), an independent school in [Hertford
Heath](/wiki/Hertford_Heath "Hertford Heath"),
[Hertfordshire](/wiki/Hertfordshire "Hertfordshire"), and later studied
[English literature](/wiki/English_literature "English literature") at
[University College London](/wiki/University_College_London "University
College London") (UCL). Opting out of a traditional film education, he pursued
"a degree in something unrelated", which his father suggested "gives a
different take on things".[20] He chose UCL specifically for its filmmaking
facilities, which comprised a [Steenbeck editing suite](/wiki/Steenbeck
"Steenbeck") and [16 mm film cameras](/wiki/16_mm_film#Cameras "16 mm
film").[21] Nolan was president of the Union's Film Society,[21] and with
[Emma Thomas](/wiki/Emma_Thomas "Emma Thomas") (his girlfriend and future
wife) he screened [feature films](/wiki/Feature_film "Feature film") in
[35mm](/wiki/35_mm_movie_film "35 mm movie film") during the school year and
used the money earned to produce 16 mm films over the summers.[22] He
graduated in 1993 with a bachelor's degree in English literature; Thomas, who
studied history at UCL and was also active in the Film Society, met Nolan on
his first day at [Ramsay
Halls](/wiki/Halls_of_residence_at_University_College_London "Halls of
residence at University College London"). They later married and co-founded
the production company [Syncopy](/wiki/Syncopy_Inc. "Syncopy Inc."). Both have
retained strong ties with UCL, receiving honorary fellowships (Nolan in 2006,
Thomas in 2013), and in 2017 Nolan was awarded an honorary doctorate.[23][24]

## Career

### 1993–2003: Early career and breakthrough

After earning his bachelor's degree in English literature in 1993, Nolan
worked as a [script reader](/wiki/Script_analyst "Script analyst"), [camera
operator](/wiki/Camera_operator "Camera operator") and director of [corporate
films](/wiki/Corporate_film "Corporate film") and [industrial
films](/wiki/Industrial_films "Industrial films").[21][25][26] He directed,
wrote and edited the short film _[Larceny](/wiki/Larceny_\(short_film\)
"Larceny \(short film\)")_ (1996),[27] which was filmed over a weekend in
black and white with limited equipment and a small cast and crew.[17][28]
Funded by Nolan and shot with the [UCL Union](/wiki/UCL_Union "UCL Union")
Film society's equipment, it appeared at the [Cambridge Film
Festival](/wiki/Cambridge_Film_Festival "Cambridge Film Festival") in 1996 and
is considered one of UCL's best shorts.[29] For unknown reasons, the film has
since been removed from public view.[27] Nolan filmed a third short,
_[Doodlebug](/wiki/Doodlebug_\(film\) "Doodlebug \(film\)")_ (1997), about a
man seemingly chasing an insect with his shoe, only to discover that it is a
miniature of himself.[20][30]

Nolan and Thomas first attempted to make a feature in the mid-1990s titled
_Larry Mahoney_ , which they scrapped.[31] During this period in his career,
Nolan had little to no success getting his projects off the ground, facing
several rejections; he added, "[T]here's a very limited pool of finance in the
UK. To be honest, it's a very clubby kind of place ... Never had any support
whatsoever from the British film industry."[32]

Shortly after abandoning _Larry Mahoney_ , Nolan conceived the idea for his
first feature, _[Following](/wiki/Following "Following")_ (1998), which he
wrote, directed, photographed and edited. The film depicts an unemployed young
writer ([Jeremy Theobald](/wiki/Jeremy_Theobald "Jeremy Theobald")) who trails
strangers through London, hoping they will provide material for his first
novel, but is drawn into a criminal underworld when he fails to keep his
distance. It was inspired by Nolan's experience of living in London and having
his apartment burgled; he observed that the common attribute between larceny
and pursuing someone through a crowd was that they both cross social
boundaries.[33] Co-produced by Nolan with Thomas and Theobald,[34] it was made
on a budget of around £3,000. Most of the cast and crew were friends of Nolan,
and shooting took place on weekends over the course of a year.[35] To conserve
[film stock](/wiki/Film_stock "Film stock"), each scene was rehearsed
extensively to ensure that the first or second take could be used in the final
edit.[20][36] _Following_ won several awards during its festival run and was
well-received by critics who labelled Nolan a majorly talented
debutant.[37][38] [Scott Timberg](/wiki/Scott_Timberg "Scott Timberg") of
_[New Times LA](/wiki/New_Times_LA "New Times LA")_ wrote that it "echoed
[Hitchcock](/wiki/Hitchcock "Hitchcock") classics", but was "leaner and
meaner".[39] [Janet Maslin](/wiki/Janet_Maslin "Janet Maslin") of _[The New
York Times](/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ was impressed with
its "spare look" and "agile hand-held camerawork", saying, "As a result, the
actors convincingly carry off the before, during and after modes that the film
eventually, and artfully, weaves together."[40]

> "The difference between shooting _[Following](/wiki/Following "Following")_
> with a group of friends wearing our own clothes and my mum making sandwiches
> to spending $4 million of somebody else's money on
> _[Memento](/wiki/Memento_\(film\) "Memento \(film\)")_ and having a crew of
> a hundred people is, to this day, by far the biggest leap I've ever made."

—Nolan on the jump from his first film to his second (2012)[41]

_Following_ 's success afforded Nolan the opportunity to make
_[Memento](/wiki/Memento_\(film\) "Memento \(film\)")_ (2000), which became
his breakthrough film. His brother Jonathan pitched the idea to him, about a
man with [anterograde amnesia](/wiki/Anterograde_amnesia "Anterograde
amnesia") who uses notes and tattoos to hunt for his wife's murderer.[42]
Jonathan worked the idea into a short story, "[Memento
Mori](/wiki/Memento_Mori_\(short_story\) "Memento Mori \(short story\)")"
(2001), and Nolan developed it into a screenplay that told the story in
reverse. Aaron Ryder, an executive for [Newmarket Films](/wiki/Newmarket_Films
"Newmarket Films"), said it was "perhaps the most innovative script I had ever
seen".[43] The film was optioned and given a budget of $4.5 million,[44] with
[Guy Pearce](/wiki/Guy_Pearce "Guy Pearce") and [Carrie-Anne
Moss](/wiki/Carrie-Anne_Moss "Carrie-Anne Moss") in the starring roles.[45]
Newmarket also distributed the film after it was rejected by studios who
feared that it would not attract a wide audience. Following a positive [word
of mouth](/wiki/Word_of_mouth "Word of mouth") and screenings in 500 theatres,
it earned $40 million.[46] _Memento_ premiered at the [Venice Film
Festival](/wiki/Venice_Film_Festival "Venice Film Festival") in September 2000
to critical acclaim.[47] [Joe Morgenstern](/wiki/Joe_Morgenstern "Joe
Morgenstern") of _[The Wall Street Journal](/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The
Wall Street Journal")_ wrote in his review, "I can't remember when a movie has
seemed so clever, strangely affecting and slyly funny at the very same
time."[48] In the book _The Philosophy of Neo-Noir_ , Basil Smith drew a
comparison with [John Locke](/wiki/John_Locke "John Locke")'s _[An Essay
Concerning Human Understanding](/wiki/An_Essay_Concerning_Human_Understanding
"An Essay Concerning Human Understanding")_ , which argues that conscious
memories constitute our identities – a theme Nolan explores in the film.[49]
_Memento_ earned Nolan many accolades, including nominations for an [Academy
Award](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Writing_\(Original_Screenplay\) "Academy
Award for Best Writing \(Original Screenplay\)") and a [Golden Globe Award for
Best Screenplay](/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Screenplay "Golden Globe
Award for Best Screenplay"), as well as two [Independent Spirit
Awards](/wiki/Independent_Spirit_Award "Independent Spirit Award"): [Best
Director](/wiki/Independent_Spirit_Award_for_Best_Director "Independent Spirit
Award for Best Director") and [Best
Screenplay](/wiki/Independent_Spirit_Award_for_Best_Screenplay "Independent
Spirit Award for Best Screenplay").[50][51] Six critics listed it as one of
the best [films of the 2000s](/wiki/2000s_in_film "2000s in film").[52] In
2001, Nolan and Emma Thomas founded the production company [Syncopy
Inc.](/wiki/Syncopy_Inc. "Syncopy Inc.")[53][b]

Impressed by his work on _Memento_ , filmmaker [Steven
Soderbergh](/wiki/Steven_Soderbergh "Steven Soderbergh") recommended Nolan to
[Warner Bros.](/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros.") to direct the [psychological
thriller](/wiki/Psychological_thriller "Psychological thriller")
_[Insomnia](/wiki/Insomnia_\(2002_film\) "Insomnia \(2002 film\)")_ (2002),
although the studio initially wanted a more seasoned director.[55] A remake of
the 1997 [Norwegian thriller of the same name](/wiki/Insomnia_\(1997_film\)
"Insomnia \(1997 film\)"), the film is viewed as "the outlier of Nolan's
filmography" due to its perceived lack of unconventionality he is known
for.[56][57] Starring [Al Pacino](/wiki/Al_Pacino "Al Pacino"), [Robin
Williams](/wiki/Robin_Williams "Robin Williams") and [Hilary
Swank](/wiki/Hilary_Swank "Hilary Swank"),[58] _Insomnia_ follows two Los
Angeles detectives sent to a northern Alaskan town to investigate the murder
of a local teenager. It received positive reviews from critics and earned $113
million against a budget of $46 million.[59][60] Film critic [Roger
Ebert](/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") praised the film for introducing new
perspectives and ideas on the issues of morality and guilt, adding, "Unlike
most remakes, the Nolan _Insomnia_ is not a pale retread, but a re-examination
of the material, like a new production of a good play."[61] [Richard
Schickel](/wiki/Richard_Schickel "Richard Schickel") of
_[Time](/wiki/Time_\(magazine\) "Time \(magazine\)")_ deemed _Insomnia_ a
"worthy successor" to _Memento_ and "a triumph of atmosphere over a none-too-
mysterious mystery".[62]

_Following_ , _Memento_ and _Insomnia_ established Nolan's image as an
"[auteur](/wiki/Auteur "Auteur")".[63] After the lattermost, he wrote a
screenplay for a [Howard Hughes](/wiki/Howard_Hughes "Howard Hughes") biopic.
Nolan reluctantly tabled his script after learning that [Martin
Scorsese](/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese") was already making one such
film: _[The Aviator](/wiki/The_Aviator_\(2004_film\) "The Aviator \(2004
film\)")_ (2004).[64] He was then briefly attached to direct a film adaptation
of [Ruth Rendell](/wiki/Ruth_Rendell "Ruth Rendell")'s novel _[The Keys to the
Street](/wiki/The_Keys_to_the_Street "The Keys to the Street")_ for [Fox
Searchlight Pictures](/wiki/Fox_Searchlight_Pictures "Fox Searchlight
Pictures") but chose to direct _[Batman Begins](/wiki/Batman_Begins "Batman
Begins")_ instead.[65] In April 2003, filmmaker [David O.
Russell](/wiki/David_O._Russell "David O. Russell") put Nolan in a
[headlock](/wiki/Grappling_hold "Grappling hold") at a Hollywood party after
learning that [Jude Law](/wiki/Jude_Law "Jude Law"), whom Russell wanted to
cast, had decided to work with Nolan instead. Russell pressured Nolan to
display "artistic solidarity" by relinquishing Law from his cast.[66][67]

### 2003–2013: Widespread recognition

In early 2003, Nolan was set to direct _[Troy](/wiki/Troy_\(film\) "Troy
\(film\)")_ (2004), based on [Homer](/wiki/Homer "Homer")'s the
_[Iliad](/wiki/Iliad "Iliad")_.[68][69][70] After leaving _Troy_ , Nolan
approached Warner Bros. with the idea of making a new [Batman](/wiki/Batman
"Batman") film, based on the character's origin story.[71] Nolan was
fascinated by the notion of grounding it in a more realistic world than a
comic-book fantasy.[72] He relied heavily on traditional [stunts](/wiki/Stunt
"Stunt") and [miniature effects](/wiki/Miniature_effect "Miniature effect")
during filming, with minimal use of [computer-generated
imagery](/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery "Computer-generated imagery")
(CGI).[73] _[Batman Begins](/wiki/Batman_Begins "Batman Begins")_ (2005), the
biggest project Nolan had undertaken to that point,[74] was released to
critical acclaim and commercial success.[75][76] Starring [Christian
Bale](/wiki/Christian_Bale "Christian Bale") as [Bruce Wayne /
Batman](/wiki/Bruce_Wayne_\(Dark_Knight_trilogy\) "Bruce Wayne \(Dark Knight
trilogy\)")—along with [Michael Caine](/wiki/Michael_Caine "Michael Caine"),
[Gary Oldman](/wiki/Gary_Oldman "Gary Oldman"), [Morgan
Freeman](/wiki/Morgan_Freeman "Morgan Freeman") and [Liam
Neeson](/wiki/Liam_Neeson "Liam Neeson")— _Batman Begins_ revived the
franchise.[77][78] _Batman Begins_ was 2005's ninth-highest-grossing film and
was praised for its psychological depth and contemporary relevance;[76][79] it
is cited as one of the most influential films of the 2000s.[80] Film author
Ian Nathan wrote that within five years of his career, Nolan "[went] from
unknown to indie darling to gaining creative control over one of the biggest
properties in Hollywood, and (perhaps unwittingly) fomenting the genre that
would redefine the entire industry".[81]

Nolan directed, co-wrote and produced _[The
Prestige](/wiki/The_Prestige_\(film\) "The Prestige \(film\)")_ (2006), an
adaptation of [the Christopher Priest novel](/wiki/The_Prestige "The
Prestige") about two rival 19th-century magicians.[82] The screenplay was the
result of an intermittent, five-year collaboration between him and his brother
Jonathan, who had begun writing it already in 2001. Nolan initially intended
to make the film as early as 2003, but had postponed the project after
agreeing to make _Batman Begins_.[83][84] Starring [Hugh
Jackman](/wiki/Hugh_Jackman "Hugh Jackman") and Christian Bale in the lead
roles of rival magicians, _The Prestige_ received critical acclaim and
received two Academy Award nominations.[85][86] Roger Ebert described it as
"quite a movie - atmospheric, obsessive, almost satanic",[87] and [Kenneth
Turan](/wiki/Kenneth_Turan "Kenneth Turan") of the _[Los Angeles
Times](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ called it an "ambitious,
unnerving melodrama".[88] _[The Guardian](/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")_
's [Philip French](/wiki/Philip_French "Philip French") wrote: "In addition to
the intellectual or philosophical excitement it engenders, _The Prestige_ is
gripping, suspenseful, mysterious, moving and often darkly funny."[89] Despite
a negative box-office prognosis, the film earned over $109 million against a
budget of $40 million.[90]

[![Christopher Nolan speaking to the mic while four people are standing behind
him](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/The_Dark_Knight_European_Premier_-
_Leicester_square2.jpg/330px-The_Dark_Knight_European_Premier_-
_Leicester_square2.jpg)](/wiki/File:The_Dark_Knight_European_Premier_-
_Leicester_square2.jpg)Nolan (left) with the cast and crew of _[The Dark
Knight](/wiki/The_Dark_Knight "The Dark Knight")_ at the 2008 European
premiere in London

_[The Dark Knight](/wiki/The_Dark_Knight "The Dark Knight")_ (2008), the
follow-up to _Batman Begins_ , was Nolan's next venture. Initially reluctant
to make a sequel, he agreed after Warner Bros. repeatedly insisted.[91] Nolan
wanted to expand on the [noir](/wiki/Film_noir "Film noir") quality of the
first film by broadening the canvas and taking on "the dynamic of a story of
the city, a large crime story ... where you're looking at the police, the
justice system, the vigilante, the poor people, the rich people, the
criminals".[92] Continuing to minimise the use of CGI, Nolan employed high-
resolution [IMAX](/wiki/IMAX "IMAX") cameras, making it the first major motion
picture to use this technology.[93][94] _The Dark Knight_ has been ranked as
one of the best films of the 2000s and one of the [best superhero films ever
made](/wiki/List_of_films_considered_the_best#Superhero "List of films
considered the best").[c] Many critics declare _The Dark Knight_ to be "the
most successful comic book film ever made".[99] [Manohla
Dargis](/wiki/Manohla_Dargis "Manohla Dargis") of _The New York Times_ found
the film to be of higher artistic merit than many Hollywood blockbusters:
"Pitched at the divide between art and industry, poetry and entertainment, it
goes darker and deeper than any Hollywood movie of its comic-book kind."[100]
Ebert expressed a similar point of view, describing it as a "haunted film that
leaps beyond its origins and becomes an engrossing tragedy".[101] _The Dark
Knight_ set many box-office records during its theatrical run,[102] earning
over $1 billion worldwide.[103] At the [81st Academy
Awards](/wiki/81st_Academy_Awards "81st Academy Awards"), the film was
nominated in eight categories, winning two: [Best Sound
Editing](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Sound_Editing "Academy Award for Best
Sound Editing") for [Richard King](/wiki/Richard_King_\(sound_designer\)
"Richard King \(sound designer\)") and a posthumous [Best Supporting Actor
award](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Academy Award for Best
Supporting Actor") for [Heath Ledger](/wiki/Heath_Ledger "Heath Ledger").[104]
The film's failure to garner a Best Picture nomination was criticised by the
media. Beginning in 2010, the
[Academy](/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences "Academy of Motion
Picture Arts and Sciences") increased their Best Picture nominees from five to
ten, a change known as "The Dark Knight Rule".[105] Nolan received many
[awards and nominations](/wiki/List_of_accolades_received_by_The_Dark_Knight
"List of accolades received by The Dark Knight") for his work on the film.[50]
In the late 2000s, Nolan was reported to direct a film adaptation of the 1960s
television series _[The Prisoner](/wiki/The_Prisoner "The
Prisoner")_.[65][106]

The success of _The Dark Knight_ allowed Warner Bros. to sign Nolan to write,
direct and co-produce _[Inception](/wiki/Inception "Inception")_ (2010) – a
film for which he had the idea around nine years before its release.[107]
Nolan described the film as "a contemporary sci-fi actioner set within the
architecture of the mind".[108] Starring a large ensemble cast led by
[Leonardo DiCaprio](/wiki/Leonardo_DiCaprio "Leonardo DiCaprio"), the film
became a critical and commercial success upon its release.[109] Film critic
[Mark Kermode](/wiki/Mark_Kermode "Mark Kermode") named it the best film of
2010, stating "_Inception_ is proof that people are not stupid, that cinema is
not trash, and that it is possible for blockbusters and art to be the same
thing."[110] Philosophy professor [David Kyle
Johnson](/wiki/David_Kyle_Johnson "David Kyle Johnson") wrote that
"_Inception_ became a classic almost as soon as it was projected on silver
screens", praising its exploration of philosophical ideas, including [leap of
faith](/wiki/Leap_of_faith "Leap of faith") and [allegory of the
cave](/wiki/Allegory_of_the_cave "Allegory of the cave").[111] The film
grossed over $836 million worldwide.[112] Nominated for eight Academy
Awards—including Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay—it won [Best
Cinematography](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Cinematography "Academy Award for
Best Cinematography"), [Best Sound Mixing](/wiki/Best_Sound_Mixing "Best Sound
Mixing"), [Best Sound Editing](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Sound_Editing
"Academy Award for Best Sound Editing") and [Best Visual
Effects](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Visual_Effects "Academy Award for Best
Visual Effects").[113] Nolan was nominated for a [BAFTA
Award](/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Direction")
and a [Golden Globe Award for Best
Director](/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Director "Golden Globe Award for
Best Director"), [among other
accolades](/wiki/List_of_accolades_received_by_Inception "List of accolades
received by Inception").[50]

[![Christopher Nolan is looking directly towards the
camera.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Christopher_Nolan%2C_London%2C_2013_%28crop%29.jpg/250px-
Christopher_Nolan%2C_London%2C_2013_%28crop%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Christopher_Nolan,_London,_2013_\(crop\).jpg)Nolan
at the 2013 premiere of _[Man of Steel](/wiki/Man_of_Steel_\(film\) "Man of
Steel \(film\)")_ in London

Around the release of _[The Dark Knight Rises](/wiki/The_Dark_Knight_Rises
"The Dark Knight Rises")_ (2012), Nolan's third and final Batman film, Joseph
Bevan of the [British Film Institute](/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British
Film Institute") wrote a profile on him: "In the space of just over a decade,
Christopher Nolan has shot from promising British indie director to undisputed
master of a new brand of intelligent escapism."[114] After initial hesitation,
Nolan agreed to return to direct _The Dark Knight Rises_ and worked with his
brother and [David S. Goyer](/wiki/David_S._Goyer "David S. Goyer") to develop
a story that he felt would end [the
trilogy](/wiki/Batman_in_film#The_Dark_Knight_trilogy "Batman in film") on a
high note.[115] The film was released to positive reviews.[116] Kenneth Turan
found the film "potent, persuasive and hypnotic" and "more than an exceptional
superhero movie, it is masterful filmmaking by any standard".[117] [Christy
Lemire](/wiki/Christy_Lemire "Christy Lemire") of _[HuffPost](/wiki/HuffPost
"HuffPost")_ wrote in her review that Nolan concluded his trilogy in a
"typically spectacular, ambitious fashion", but disliked the "overloaded"
story and excessive grimness.[118] _The Dark Knight Rises_ was a box office
success, becoming the thirteenth film to gross $1 billion.[119] During a
midnight showing of the film in [Aurora, Colorado](/wiki/Aurora,_Colorado
"Aurora, Colorado"), [a gunman opened fire inside the
theatre](/wiki/2012_Aurora,_Colorado_shooting "2012 Aurora, Colorado
shooting"), killing 12 people and injuring 58 others.[120] Nolan released a
statement expressing his condolences for the victims of what he described as a
"senseless tragedy".[121]

_The Dark Knight_ trilogy inspired a trend in future superhero films seeking
to replicate its gritty, realistic tone to little success. The second
instalment in particular revitalised the genre at a time when recent superhero
films had failed to meet expectations.[122][123] Ben Child of _The Guardian_
wrote that the three films "will remain thrilling totems of the genre for
decades to come".[122] During story discussions for _The Dark Knight Rises_ ,
Goyer told Nolan of his idea about _[Man of Steel](/wiki/Man_of_Steel_\(film\)
"Man of Steel \(film\)")_ (2013), which the latter would produce.[124]
Impressed with [Zack Snyder](/wiki/Zack_Snyder "Zack Snyder")'s work in
_[300](/wiki/300_\(film\) "300 \(film\)")_ (2006) and
_[Watchmen](/wiki/Watchmen_\(2009_film\) "Watchmen \(2009 film\)")_ (2009),
Nolan hired him to direct the film.[125] Starring [Henry
Cavill](/wiki/Henry_Cavill "Henry Cavill") as [Clark
Kent](/wiki/Superman_\(DC_Extended_Universe\) "Superman \(DC Extended
Universe\)") who learns that he is a powerful alien, _Man of Steel_ received
mixed reviews and grossed more than $660 million against a budget of $220
million.[126][127]

### 2014–2019: _Interstellar_ , _Dunkirk_ and other activities

[![Jonathan Nolan looking to his
left](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Jonathan_Nolan_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg/250px-
Jonathan_Nolan_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg)](/wiki/File:Jonathan_Nolan_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg)Nolan
and his younger brother, [Jonathan](/wiki/Jonathan_Nolan "Jonathan Nolan")
(_pictured_ in 2017), wrote several screenplays together, including that of
_Interstellar_.

Nolan next directed, wrote and produced the science-fiction film
_[Interstellar](/wiki/Interstellar_\(film\) "Interstellar \(film\)")_ (2014).
The first drafts of the script were written by Jonathan Nolan, and it was
originally to be directed by [Steven Spielberg](/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven
Spielberg").[128] Based on the scientific theories of [theoretical
physicist](/wiki/Theoretical_physicist "Theoretical physicist") [Kip
Thorne](/wiki/Kip_Thorne "Kip Thorne"), the film follows a group of
[astronauts](/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") who travel through a
[wormhole](/wiki/Wormhole "Wormhole") in search of a new home for
humanity.[129] In a 2014 discussion of the film's physics, Nolan expressed his
admiration for [scientific objectivity](/wiki/Scientific_objectivity
"Scientific objectivity"), wishing it were applied "in every aspect of our
civilisation".[130] _Interstellar_ – starring [Matthew
McConaughey](/wiki/Matthew_McConaughey "Matthew McConaughey"), [Anne
Hathaway](/wiki/Anne_Hathaway "Anne Hathaway") and [Jessica
Chastain](/wiki/Jessica_Chastain "Jessica Chastain") – was released to
positive reviews and grossed $773 million worldwide.[131][132] Observing its
"visual dazzle, thematic ambition", _The New York Times_ 's [A. O.
Scott](/wiki/A._O._Scott "A. O. Scott") wrote that _Interstellar_ is a
"sweeping, futuristic adventure driven by grief, dread and regret".[133]
Documentary filmmaker [Toni Myers](/wiki/Toni_Myers "Toni Myers") called the
film "a real work of art" and praised it for exploring a story spanning
multiple generations.[134] _Interstellar_ was particularly praised for its
scientific accuracy, which led to the publication of two [academic
papers](/wiki/Scientific_papers "Scientific papers").[135][136] The _[American
Journal of Physics](/wiki/American_Journal_of_Physics "American Journal of
Physics")_ called for it to be shown in school science lessons.[137][138] At
the [87th Academy Awards](/wiki/87th_Academy_Awards "87th Academy Awards"),
the film won Best Visual Effects and received four other nominations.[139]
Also in 2014, Nolan and Emma Thomas served as executive producers on
_[Transcendence](/wiki/Transcendence_\(2014_film\) "Transcendence \(2014
film\)")_ , the directorial debut of his longtime cinematographer [Wally
Pfister](/wiki/Wally_Pfister "Wally Pfister").[140]

In the mid-2010s, Nolan took part in several ventures for film preservation
and distribution of the work of lesser-known filmmakers. His production
company, Syncopy, formed a joint venture with [Zeitgeist
Films](/wiki/Zeitgeist_Films "Zeitgeist Films") to release [Blu-
ray](/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") editions of Zeitgeist's films.[141] As a part of
the Blu-ray release of the animation films of the [Brothers
Quay](/wiki/Brothers_Quay "Brothers Quay"), Nolan directed the documentary
short _[Quay](/wiki/Quay_\(film\) "Quay \(film\)")_ (2015). He initiated a
theatrical tour, showcasing the Quays' _[In
Absentia](/wiki/In_Absentia_\(film\) "In Absentia \(film\)")_ , _The Comb_ and
_[Street of Crocodiles](/wiki/Street_of_Crocodiles "Street of Crocodiles")_.
[IndieWire](/wiki/IndieWire "IndieWire") wrote that the brothers "will
undoubtedly have hundreds, if not thousands more fans because of Nolan, and
for that _The Quay Brothers in 35mm_ will always be one of [the] latter's most
important contributions to cinema".[142][143] An advocate for the survival of
the analogue medium, Nolan and visual artist [Tacita Dean](/wiki/Tacita_Dean
"Tacita Dean") invited representatives from leading American film archives,
laboratories and presenting institutions to participate in an informal summit
entitled _Reframing the Future of Film_ at the [Getty
Museum](/wiki/Getty_Museum "Getty Museum") in March 2015.[144][145] Subsequent
events were held at [Tate Modern](/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern") in London,
[Museo Tamayo](/wiki/Museo_Rufino_Tamayo,_Mexico_City "Museo Rufino Tamayo,
Mexico City") in Mexico City and [Tata Theatre](/wiki/Tata_Theatre "Tata
Theatre") in [Mumbai](/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai").[146] In April 2015, Nolan joined
the board of directors of [The Film Foundation](/wiki/The_Film_Foundation "The
Film Foundation"), a non-profitable organisation dedicated to [film
preservation](/wiki/Film_preservation "Film preservation"),[147] and was
appointed, along with Martin Scorsese, by the [Library of
Congress](/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") to serve on the
[National Film Preservation Board](/wiki/National_Film_Preservation_Board
"National Film Preservation Board") as DGA representatives.[148] Nolan serves
on the [Motion Picture & Television
Fund](/wiki/Motion_Picture_%26_Television_Fund "Motion Picture & Television
Fund") Board of Governors.[149]

After serving as an executive producer on Zack Snyder's _[Batman v Superman:
Dawn of Justice](/wiki/Batman_v_Superman:_Dawn_of_Justice "Batman v Superman:
Dawn of Justice")_ (2016) and _[Justice League](/wiki/Justice_League_\(film\)
"Justice League \(film\)")_ (2017),[150][151] Nolan returned to directing with
_[Dunkirk](/wiki/Dunkirk_\(2017_film\) "Dunkirk \(2017 film\)")_ (2017). Based
on his own original screenplay and co-produced with Thomas, the film is set
amid World War II in 1940 and the [evacuation](/wiki/Dunkirk_evacuation
"Dunkirk evacuation") of [Allied](/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of
World War II") soldiers from the beaches of [Dunkirk](/wiki/Dunkirk
"Dunkirk"), France. Describing the film as a survival tale with a
[triptych](/wiki/Triptych "Triptych") structure, Nolan wanted to make a
"sensory, almost experimental movie" with minimal dialogue.[152] He said he
waited to make _Dunkirk_ until he had earned the trust of a major studio to
let him make it as a British film but with an American budget.[153] Before
filming, Nolan sought advice from Spielberg, who later said in an interview
with _[Variety](/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety \(magazine\)")_ , "knowing
and respecting that Chris [Nolan] is one of the world's most imaginative
filmmakers, my advice to him was to leave his imagination, as I did on
_[Ryan](/wiki/Saving_Private_Ryan "Saving Private Ryan")_ , in second position
to the research he was doing to authentically acquit this historical
drama".[154] Starring an ensemble cast,[155] _Dunkirk_ was released to
widespread critical acclaim and strong box office results.[156][157][158] It
grossed over $526 million worldwide, making it the highest-grossing World War
II film of all time.[159] In his review, [Mick LaSalle](/wiki/Mick_LaSalle
"Mick LaSalle") of the _[San Francisco
Chronicle](/wiki/San_Francisco_Chronicle "San Francisco Chronicle")_ wrote:
"It's one of the best [war films](/wiki/War_film "War film") ever made,
distinct in its look, in its approach and in the effect it has on viewers.
There are movies—they are rare—that lift you out of your present circumstances
and immerse you so fully in another experience that you watch in a state of
jaw-dropped awe. _Dunkirk_ is that kind of movie."[160] The film received
[many accolades](/wiki/List_of_accolades_received_by_Dunkirk "List of
accolades received by Dunkirk"), including Nolan's first Oscar nomination for
[Best Director](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director "Academy Award for Best
Director").[161]

[![A picture showing five people standing on a red
carpet](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Cannes_2018_4.jpg/330px-
Cannes_2018_4.jpg)](/wiki/File:Cannes_2018_4.jpg)Nolan (right) with [Keir
Dullea](/wiki/Keir_Dullea "Keir Dullea"), Katharina Kubrick, Ron Sanders and
[Jan Harlan](/wiki/Jan_Harlan "Jan Harlan") at the [2018 Cannes Film
Festival](/wiki/2018_Cannes_Film_Festival "2018 Cannes Film Festival")

In 2018, Nolan supervised a new [70 mm](/wiki/70_mm_film "70 mm film") print
of [Stanley Kubrick](/wiki/Stanley_Kubrick "Stanley Kubrick")'s _2001: A Space
Odyssey_ (1968), made from the [original camera
negative](/wiki/Original_camera_negative "Original camera negative"); he
presented it at the [2018 Cannes Film
Festival](/wiki/2018_Cannes_Film_Festival "2018 Cannes Film Festival").[162]
_[USA Today](/wiki/USA_Today "USA Today")_ observed that festival-goers
greeted Nolan "like a rock star with a standing ovation".[163] A year later,
Nolan and Thomas received executive producer credits on _[The Doll's
Breath](/wiki/The_Doll%27s_Breath "The Doll's Breath")_ (2019), an animated
short directed by the Quay brothers.[164]

### 2020–present: _Tenet_ , _Oppenheimer_ and _The Odyssey_

Nolan's next film was the science fiction film _[Tenet](/wiki/Tenet_\(film\)
"Tenet \(film\)")_ (2020), described by [Tom Shone](/wiki/Tom_Shone "Tom
Shone") of _[The Sunday Times](/wiki/The_Sunday_Times "The Sunday Times")_ as
"a globe-spinning riff on all things Nolanesque".[165] Nolan had worked on the
screenplay for more than five years after deliberating about its central ideas
for over a decade.[166] Delayed three times due to the [COVID-19
pandemic](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), _Tenet_ was the first
Hollywood [tent-pole](/wiki/Tent-pole_\(entertainment\) "Tent-pole
\(entertainment\)") to open in theatres after the pandemic shutdown.[167] The
film tells the story of an unnamed protagonist (played by [John David
Washington](/wiki/John_David_Washington "John David Washington")) who travels
through time to stop a world-threatening attack.[168] It grossed $363 million
worldwide on a production budget of $200 million, becoming Nolan's first to
underperform at the box-office.[169] _Tenet_ was described as his most
polarising film; critics praised the ambition and technical aspects but found
its story confusing.[170][161] [Peter Bradshaw](/wiki/Peter_Bradshaw "Peter
Bradshaw") of _The Guardian_ awarded it five out of five, calling it "a
cerebral [cadenza](/wiki/Cadenza "Cadenza"), a deadpan flourish of crazy
implausibility—but supercharged with steroidal energy and imagination".[171]
Leslie Felperin of _[The Hollywood Reporter](/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The
Hollywood Reporter")_ described it as "a chilly, cerebral film—easy to admire,
especially since it's so rich in audacity and originality, but almost
impossible to love, lacking as it is in a certain humanity".[172] At the [93rd
Academy Awards](/wiki/93rd_Academy_Awards "93rd Academy Awards"), the film won
Best Visual Effects and was nominated for [Best Production
Design](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Production_Design "Academy Award for Best
Production Design").[173] Following the release of _Tenet_ , Nolan joined the
Advisory Board of the [Society of Motion Picture and Television
Engineers](/wiki/Society_of_Motion_Picture_and_Television_Engineers "Society
of Motion Picture and Television Engineers").[174] He served as an executive
producer on _[Zack Snyder's Justice
League](/wiki/Zack_Snyder%27s_Justice_League "Zack Snyder's Justice League")_
(2021), a [director's cut](/wiki/Director%27s_cut "Director's cut") of 2017's
_Justice League_.[175]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/ChrisNolanBFI150224_%2810_of_12%29_%2853532289710%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-
ChrisNolanBFI150224_%2810_of_12%29_%2853532289710%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:ChrisNolanBFI150224_\(10_of_12\)_\(53532289710\)_\(cropped\).jpg)Nolan
at [BFI Southbank](/wiki/BFI_Southbank "BFI Southbank") in 2024

Nolan's 12th film was _[Oppenheimer](/wiki/Oppenheimer_\(film\) "Oppenheimer
\(film\)")_ (2023), a biopic based on [J. Robert
Oppenheimer](/wiki/J._Robert_Oppenheimer "J. Robert Oppenheimer") (played by
[Cillian Murphy](/wiki/Cillian_Murphy "Cillian Murphy")) and his role in the
development of the [atom bomb](/wiki/Atom_bomb "Atom bomb").[176] It was
Nolan's first [R-rated](/wiki/Motion_Picture_Association_film_rating_system
"Motion Picture Association film rating system") film since _Insomnia_
(2002).[177] The film was financed and distributed by [Universal
Pictures](/wiki/Universal_Pictures "Universal Pictures"), making it Nolan's
first feature film since _Memento_ that was not made for Warner Bros. He
disagreed with Warner Bros.' decision to simultaneously release their films in
theatres and on [HBO Max](/wiki/HBO_Max "HBO Max").[178] Nolan secured the
deal with Universal after he was promised a production budget of around $100
million with an equal marketing budget, total creative control, 20% of [first-
dollar gross](/wiki/First-dollar_gross "First-dollar gross"), a 100-day
theatrical window and a blackout period from the studio wherein the company
would not release another film three weeks before or after _Oppenheimer_ 's
release.[179] The film received critical acclaim.[180] Matthew Jackson of
_[The A.V. Club](/wiki/The_A.V._Club "The A.V. Club")_ wrote, "_Oppenheimer_
deserves the title of masterpiece. It's Christopher Nolan's best film so far,
a step up to a new level for one of our finest filmmakers, and a movie that
burns itself into your brain."[181] Terming it "boldly imaginative and
[Nolan's] most mature work yet", [BBC Culture](/wiki/BBC_Culture "BBC
Culture")'s [Caryn James](/wiki/Caryn_James "Caryn James") added that it
combined the "explosive, commercially-enticing action of _The Dark Knight_
trilogy" with the "cerebral underpinnings" of _Memento_ , _Inception_ and
_Tenet_.[182] _Oppenheimer_ grossed over $975 million worldwide, making it the
[third-highest-grossing film of 2023](/wiki/2023_in_film#Highest-
grossing_films "2023 in film").[183] Among the film's [numerous
accolades](/wiki/List_of_accolades_received_by_Oppenheimer_\(film\) "List of
accolades received by Oppenheimer \(film\)"),[184][185] Nolan won the Academy
Awards for Best Director and Best Picture.[186]

As of February 2025, Nolan will once again work with Universal Studios on
_[The Odyssey](/wiki/The_Odyssey_\(2026_film\) "The Odyssey \(2026 film\)")_ ,
an adaptation of the [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek "Ancient Greek")
[epic poem](/wiki/Epic_poem "Epic poem") the _[Odyssey](/wiki/Odyssey
"Odyssey")_ by [Homer](/wiki/Homer "Homer"). It is scheduled to be released in
July 2026.[187] It follows [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") (portrayed by
[Matt Damon](/wiki/Matt_Damon "Matt Damon")), the legendary
[Greek](/wiki/Greeks "Greeks") king of [Ithaca](/wiki/Homer%27s_Ithaca
"Homer's Ithaca"), on his perilous journey to return home following the
[Trojan War](/wiki/Trojan_War "Trojan War"), his encounters with the cyclops
[Polyphemus](/wiki/Polyphemus "Polyphemus"), [the Sirens](/wiki/The_Sirens
"The Sirens"), and the witch goddess [Circe](/wiki/Circe "Circe"), and his
reunion with his wife, [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope").[188] With an
estimated production budget of $250 million, it is poised to be the most
expensive film of Nolan's career.[189] The film will be the first mainstream
blockbuster to be shot entirely on IMAX film.[190][191] Nolan was elected
president of the [Directors Guild of America](/wiki/Directors_Guild_of_America
"Directors Guild of America"), a labour organisation representing more than
19,500 members, in September 2025.[192]

## Personal life and public image

[![Christopher Nolan, on the right, is looking directly towards the camera as
Emma Thomas is looking to her
right.](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Christopher_Nolan_and_Emma_Thomas.jpg/250px-
Christopher_Nolan_and_Emma_Thomas.jpg)](/wiki/File:Christopher_Nolan_and_Emma_Thomas.jpg)Nolan
and his wife [Emma Thomas](/wiki/Emma_Thomas "Emma Thomas") in January 2011.
Thomas has worked as a producer on all of Nolan's films since 1997.

Nolan is married to [Emma Thomas](/wiki/Emma_Thomas "Emma Thomas"), whom he
met at [University College London](/wiki/University_College_London "University
College London") when he was 19.[14][22] She has worked as a producer on all
of his films since 1997.[53][193] The couple have four children and reside in
Los Angeles.[194] Nolan and Thomas were included in the _[Sunday Times Rich
List](/wiki/Sunday_Times_Rich_List "Sunday Times Rich List")_ of
[2025](/wiki/Sunday_Times_Rich_List_2025 "Sunday Times Rich List 2025") with
an estimated [net worth](/wiki/Net_worth "Net worth") of £360 million.[195]

Nolan prefers to maintain a certain level of mystery about his work.[196]
Refusing to discuss his personal life,[197] he feels that too much
biographical information about a filmmaker detracts from the experience of his
audiences. He stated, "I actually don't want people to have me in mind at all
when they're watching the films."[196] He does not own a smartphone or have an
email address, preferring to hand-deliver his scripts to actors instead and
have his wife handle outreach with producers and distributors.[198]

## Filmmaking style

Main article: [Cinematic style of Christopher
Nolan](/wiki/Cinematic_style_of_Christopher_Nolan "Cinematic style of
Christopher Nolan")

Nolan's films are largely centred in [metaphysical](/wiki/Metaphysical
"Metaphysical") themes, exploring the concepts of [time](/wiki/Time "Time"),
[memory](/wiki/Memory "Memory") and [personal
identity](/wiki/Personal_identity "Personal identity").[199][200] His work is
characterised by [mathematically inspired](/wiki/Mathematics_and_art
"Mathematics and art") ideas and images, unconventional [narrative
structures](/wiki/Nonlinear_narrative "Nonlinear narrative"),
[materialistic](/wiki/Materialism "Materialism") perspectives, and evocative
use of music and sound.[d] Filmmaker [Guillermo del
Toro](/wiki/Guillermo_del_Toro "Guillermo del Toro") called Nolan "an
emotional mathematician".[205] [BBC](/wiki/BBC "BBC")'s arts editor [Will
Gompertz](/wiki/Will_Gompertz "Will Gompertz") described him as "an art house
auteur making intellectually ambitious blockbuster movies that can leave your
pulse racing and your head spinning".[206] Joseph Bevan wrote, "His films
allow arthouse regulars to enjoy superhero flicks and multiplex crowds to
engage with labyrinthine plot conceits."[114] Nolan views himself as "an indie
filmmaker working inside the studio system".[207]

> "Christopher Nolan doesn't make sense. And that is exactly how he likes it.
> In twenty-three years and through twelve films, he has defied the laws of
> Hollywood by creating startling, original genre pieces that have revelled in
> their own complexity, confounding every maxim by which the studios hope to
> appeal to the widest audience. And yet he does that too. Cinemas fill on the
> possibility of the next Nolan film. Whatever form it might take."

—Film author Ian Nathan on Nolan as a filmmaker (2022)[208]

In the sixteen-essay book _The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan_ , professional
philosophers and writers analysed Nolan's work; they identified themes of
self-destruction, the nature and value of the truth, and the political mindset
of the hero and villain, among others.[209] Robbie B. H. Goh, a professor of
English literature, described Nolan as a "philosophical filmmaker" who
includes philosophical ideas—[existentialism](/wiki/Existentialism
"Existentialism"), [morality](/wiki/Morality "Morality"),
[epistemology](/wiki/Epistemology "Epistemology") and the distinction between
appearance and reality—in films that frequently portray suspense, action and
violence. Goh appreciated his ability to incorporate such themes in films that
possess "elements of the Hollywood blockbuster"—which help keep the audiences
engaged—but simultaneously remain "more thoughtful and self-reflexive than the
typical consumerist action film".[210] He further wrote that Nolan's body of
work reflect "a heterogeneity of conditions of products" extending from low-
budget films to lucrative blockbusters, "a wide range of genres and settings"
and "a diversity of styles that trumpet his versatility".[211]

[David Bordwell](/wiki/David_Bordwell "David Bordwell"), a [film
theorist](/wiki/Film_theorist "Film theorist"), wrote that Nolan has been able
to blend his "experimental impulses" with the demands of mainstream
entertainment, describing his oeuvre as "experiments with cinematic time by
means of techniques of subjective viewpoint and crosscutting".[212] Nolan's
use of practical, in-camera effects, miniatures and models, as well as
shooting on celluloid film, has been highly influential in early [21st century
cinema](/wiki/Hollywood_cinema_in_21st_century "Hollywood cinema in 21st
century").[213][214] IndieWire wrote in 2019 that Nolan "kept a viable
alternate model of big-budget filmmaking alive", in an era where blockbuster
filmmaking has become "a largely computer-generated art form".[214] Because of
Nolan's deep involvement in the technical facet of his films, Stuart Joy
described him as a "complete filmmaker", who "oversees all aspects of
production while also managing cultural and industrial factors outside of the
text".[215]

## Recognition

Nolan has made some of the most influential and popular films of his time.[e]
Many of his films have been regarded by critics as among the best of their
respective decades,[52][220][221] and according to _The Wall Street Journal_ ,
his "ability to combine box-office success with artistic ambition has given
him an extraordinary amount of clout in the industry".[222] His films have
earned more than $6 billion.[223] Nolan's films _Memento_ and _The Dark
Knight_ have been selected by the US Library of Congress to be preserved in
the [National Film Registry](/wiki/National_Film_Registry "National Film
Registry") for being "culturally, historically or aesthetically"
significant.[224][225] These films and _Inception_ appeared in [BBC's 100
Greatest Films of the 21st
Century](/wiki/BBC%27s_100_Greatest_Films_of_the_21st_Century "BBC's 100
Greatest Films of the 21st Century") and _The Hollywood Reporter_ 's poll of
best films ever made.[226][227] In 2017, _The Dark Knight_ , _Inception_ and
_Interstellar_ featured in _[Empire](/wiki/Empire_\(magazine\) "Empire
\(magazine\)")_ magazine's poll of "The 100 Greatest Movies".[228] In 2018,
_The Hollywood Reporter_ listed Nolan as one of the 100 most powerful people
in entertainment and described him as a "franchise unto himself".[229]
_[Parade](/wiki/Parade_\(magazine\) "Parade \(magazine\)")_ ranked Nolan
number eight in its 2022 list of 75 Best Movie Directors of All Time.[230]

[![Four-color National Film Registry logo on black
background](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/National_Film_Registry_logo_vector.svg/250px-
National_Film_Registry_logo_vector.svg.png)](/wiki/File:National_Film_Registry_logo_vector.svg)Two
of Nolan's films (_[Memento](/wiki/Memento_\(film\) "Memento \(film\)")_ and
_[The Dark Knight](/wiki/The_Dark_Knight "The Dark Knight")_) have been
selected by the [Library of Congress](/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of
Congress") for preservation in the [National Film
Registry](/wiki/National_Film_Registry "National Film Registry").[224][225]

Nolan's work has been as "intensely embraced, analysed and debated by ordinary
film fans as by critics and film academics".[197][231] Calling him "a
persuasively inventive storyteller", [Geoff Andrew](/wiki/Geoff_Andrew "Geoff
Andrew") of the British Film Institute named Nolan one of the few contemporary
filmmakers producing highly personal films within the Hollywood mainstream.
Andrew wrote that Nolan's films are "not so much [notable] for their
considerable technical virtuosity and visual flair as for their brilliant
narrative ingenuity and their unusually adult interest in complex
philosophical questions".[232] David Bordwell observed that Nolan is
"considered one of the most accomplished living filmmakers", citing his
ability to turn genre movies into both art and event films, as well as his box
office numbers, critical acclaim and popularity among cinemagoers.[212][233]
In 2008, [Philip French](/wiki/Philip_French "Philip French") deemed Nolan
"the first major talent to emerge this century".[234] [Mark
Kermode](/wiki/Mark_Kermode "Mark Kermode") complimented Nolan for bringing
"the discipline and ethics of art-house independent moviemaking and apply[ing]
them to Hollywood blockbusters. He's living proof that you don't have to
appeal to the lowest common denominator to be profitable".[235] _[The
Observer](/wiki/The_Observer "The Observer")_ 's Ryan Gilbey described Nolan
as a "skillful, stylish storyteller, capable of combining the spectacle of
Spielberg with the intellectual intricacy of [Nicolas Roeg](/wiki/Nicolas_Roeg
"Nicolas Roeg") or [Alain Resnais](/wiki/Alain_Resnais "Alain Resnais")".[236]
[Mark Cousins](/wiki/Mark_Cousins_\(film_critic\) "Mark Cousins \(film
critic\)") applauded Nolan for embracing big ideas, "Hollywood filmmakers
generally shy away from ideas—but not Christopher Nolan".[237] Scott Foundas
of _Variety_ declared Nolan "the premier big-canvas storyteller of his
generation",[238] and [Justin Chang](/wiki/Justin_Chang "Justin Chang") of the
_Los Angeles Times_ called him "the great [proceduralist](/wiki/Proceduralist
"Proceduralist") of 21st century blockbuster filmmaking, a lover of nuts-and-
bolts minutiae".[239]

Nolan has been praised by many of his contemporaries, and his work has
influenced them.[240][241][242] [Kenneth Branagh](/wiki/Kenneth_Branagh
"Kenneth Branagh") called Nolan's approach to large-scale filmmaking "unique
in modern cinema", adding, "regardless of how popular his movies become, he
remains an artist and an auteur. I think for that reason he has become a
heroic figure for both the audience and the people working behind the
camera."[243] [Michael Mann](/wiki/Michael_Mann "Michael Mann") complimented
Nolan for his "singular vision" and credited with "invent[ing] the post-heroic
superhero".[244] Nicolas Roeg said of Nolan, "People talk about 'commercial
art' and the term is usually self-negating; Nolan works in the commercial
arena and yet there's something very poetic about his work."[245] [Martin
Scorsese](/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese") identified Nolan as a
filmmaker creating "beautifully made films on a big scale".[246]

[Damien Chazelle](/wiki/Damien_Chazelle "Damien Chazelle") lauded Nolan for
his ability "to make the most seemingly impersonal projects—superhero epics,
deep-space mind-benders—feel deeply personal".[247] Discussing the difference
between [art films](/wiki/Art_film "Art film") and big studio blockbusters,
Steven Spielberg referred to Nolan's _Dark Knight_ series as an example of
both;[248] he has described _Memento_ and _Inception_ as "masterworks".[249]
[Denis Villeneuve](/wiki/Denis_Villeneuve "Denis Villeneuve") was impressed by
Nolan's ability "to keep his identity and create his own universe in that
large scope ... To bring intellectual concepts and to bring them in that scope
to the screen right now—it's very rare. Every movie that he comes out with, I
have more admiration for his work."[250] [James Cameron](/wiki/James_Cameron
"James Cameron") expressed disappointment that Nolan was not nominated for an
Academy Award as Best Director for _Inception_ , calling it "the most
astounding piece of film creation and direction of the year, hands
down".[249][251]

Nolan has been nominated for eight [Academy Awards](/wiki/Academy_Award
"Academy Award") (winning two), eight [British Academy Film
Awards](/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Awards "British Academy Film Awards")
(winning two) and six [Golden Globe Awards](/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award "Golden
Globe Award") (winning one).[50][252][253][254] From 2011 to 2014, he appeared
in [_Forbes_ Celebrity 100](/wiki/Forbes_Celebrity_100 "Forbes Celebrity 100")
list based on his income and popularity.[255] Nolan appeared in
_[Time](/wiki/Time_\(magazine\) "Time \(magazine\)")_ 's [100 most influential
people in the world](/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") in 2015.[256]

Nolan was named an Honorary Fellow of UCL in 2006,[257] and conferred an
[honorary doctorate](/wiki/Honorary_doctorate "Honorary doctorate") in
literature in 2017.[258] In 2012, he became the youngest director to receive a
hand-and-footprint ceremony at [Grauman's Chinese
Theatre](/wiki/Grauman%27s_Chinese_Theatre "Grauman's Chinese Theatre") in Los
Angeles.[259] He was appointed Commander of the [Order of the British
Empire](/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") in
the [2019 New Year Honours](/wiki/2019_New_Year_Honours "2019 New Year
Honours") for services to film.[260] In 2023, he was awarded the [Federation
of American Scientists](/wiki/Federation_of_American_Scientists "Federation of
American Scientists")' Public Service Award for his depiction of scientists in
his film _Oppenheimer_.[261] In 2024, Nolan received the [British Film
Institute Fellowship](/wiki/British_Film_Institute_Fellowship "British Film
Institute Fellowship") in recognition of his "extraordinary achievements and
enormous contribution to cinema,"[262] and the [Honorary
César](/wiki/Honorary_C%C3%A9sar "Honorary César") award from the [Académie
des Arts et Techniques du
Cinéma](/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_des_Arts_et_Techniques_du_Cin%C3%A9ma "Académie
des Arts et Techniques du Cinéma") for "continually push[ing] the boundaries
of storytelling."[263] In March 2024, Nolan was made a [knight
bachelor](/wiki/Knight_bachelor "Knight bachelor") for his contributions to
film, while his wife Emma Thomas was honoured with a damehood.[264][265]
